definition: Land, everything permanently attached to it, and the bundle of legal rights that come with owning it.
Movable items not permanently attached to land. Also called chattels or personalty.
An item that was personal property but is now attached to real property so that it is treated as part of the real estate.
Equipment a commercial tenant attaches for business use. It stays the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease ends.
Annual crops produced by a tenant's labor. They are personal property, and the tenant may return to harvest them if the tenancy ends early through no fault of their own.
The rights of an owner: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
Detaching something from the land, which turns real property into personal property, such as cutting standing timber.
Attaching personal property to land so that it becomes real property.
The written document used to transfer ownership of personal property.
A description that identifies a parcel precisely enough that a surveyor could locate it. A street address is not enough.
A legal description that follows a parcel's boundaries by distance and direction, starting and ending at the point of beginning.
The fixed starting point of a metes and bounds description. The description must return to it to close the parcel.
A legal description that identifies a parcel by lot and block number on a subdivision plat recorded with the county. Also called the recorded plat system.
The government survey system that divides land into townships and sections using meridians and base lines.
In the rectangular survey system, a square of land 6 miles on each side, containing 36 sections.
One square mile of land in the rectangular survey system, containing 640 acres.
A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet.
The economic characteristic that people prefer some locations over others, which drives value.
The physical characteristic that no two parcels of land are identical. Also called nonhomogeneity.
Any claim, right, or interest in a property held by someone other than the owner that may lower its value or limit its use.
A claim against property that secures payment of a debt. Every lien is an encumbrance.
A lien against one particular property, such as a mortgage, property tax lien, or mechanic's lien.
A lien against all of a debtor's property, such as a judgment lien or a federal tax lien.
A specific lien filed by someone who supplied labor or materials to improve a property and was not paid.
An easement that benefits a neighboring parcel. It runs with the land and transfers automatically when either parcel is sold.
An easement that benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel, such as a utility easement.
The parcel that benefits from an easement appurtenant.
The parcel burdened by an easement, which must allow the use.
An easement created by law to give a landlocked parcel access to a road.
Personal, revocable permission to enter or use land for a specific purpose. It is not an interest in the land.
An improvement, such as a fence or garage, that extends onto a neighbor's property. Usually revealed by a survey.
A recorded notice that a lawsuit affecting title to a property is pending.
The degree, quantity, and duration of a person's interest in real property.
An ownership estate of indefinite duration, such as a fee simple or life estate.
The most complete form of ownership: unlimited duration, inheritable, and with no conditions attached.
A fee estate that can be lost if a stated condition is broken. Includes fee simple determinable and fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.
A freehold estate that lasts for the lifetime of a named person.
A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant.
A third party named to receive the property when a life estate ends.
The return of property to the original grantor or their heirs when a life estate ends and no remainderman was named.
Damage or neglect by a life tenant or tenant that lowers the property's value for those who own the future interest.
A tenant's non-freehold interest in property for the term of a lease.
A leasehold with a definite start and end date. It ends on its own without notice.
A leasehold that renews automatically for successive periods, such as month to month, until either party gives notice.
A leasehold of no fixed length that either party may end at any time with proper notice.
The status of a tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent.
Ownership by one person or one legal entity alone.
Co-ownership of undivided interests that may be unequal, with no right of survivorship. Each share passes to the owner's heirs or devisees.
Co-ownership with equal shares and right of survivorship. It requires the four unities of possession, interest, time, and title.
When a co-owner dies, their interest passes automatically to the surviving co-owners rather than to heirs.
Possession, interest, time, and title: the four conditions required to create a joint tenancy.
A court action that divides co-owned property, or orders it sold, when the co-owners cannot agree.
An arrangement in which a trustor transfers property to a trustee, who holds legal title for the benefit of a beneficiary.
A business entity whose members have limited personal liability and can choose pass-through taxation.
A partnership with at least one general partner who manages and is fully liable, and limited partners whose risk is limited to their investment.
Ownership of a unit in fee simple plus an undivided interest in the common elements shared with the other unit owners.
The parts of a condominium owned together by all unit owners, such as the land, hallways, roof, and pool.
Common elements reserved for one or a few units, such as an assigned parking space or a balcony.
The recorded document that creates a condominium or planned community and sets its rules.
A building owned by a corporation. Residents buy shares in the corporation and receive a proprietary lease to their unit.
The lease a cooperative shareholder receives that gives them the right to occupy a specific unit.
A development where owners hold title to their own lot and home while an association owns the common areas.
A real property ownership interest in a unit for a recurring period of time.
A right to use a unit for a set period, without an ownership interest in the real estate.
A charge an owners' association levies on owners to pay for shared expenses and reserves.
